title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
hook: in the ruins, the mercies of the Lord are not consumed

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new covenant: the law moved from stone into the innermost part of a person. Your line was written on the heart.

Here's a strange fact about grief: someone once wrote it out in alphabetical order. The Book of Lamentations is five poems about Jerusalem after the Babylonians burned it. The walls are down, the Temple is ash, children beg for bread in the streets. And four of the five poems are acrostics: each verse, or each set of verses, starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav. Maybe it was a way to hold sorrow that has no shape. And right in the middle of the middle poem, something turns.
screen: `GRIEF IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER.` → `A CITY IN ASHES.` → `IN THE MIDDLE, SOMETHING TURNS.`

segments.voice: Chapter three is the longest poem, sixty-six verses, three for each letter. A man says, in effect: I am the one who has seen affliction. He's been walled in, weighed down with chains, his prayers shut out, his teeth broken on gravel. His hope, he says, has perished. Then at verse twenty-one: this I call back to mind, and so I have hope. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "The mercies of the Lord that we are not consumed: because his commiserations have not failed. They are new every morning, great is thy faithfulness." Commiserations is an old word for compassion. In Hebrew it's rachamim, which shares its root with the word for womb, and some readers hear a mother's love in it. Notice what the poet doesn't say. He doesn't say the city is fine. The ruins are still there when he looks up. He says the mercies are not used up. Like manna in the desert, they don't keep overnight; they come new each morning, enough for the day. Tradition gives the book to Jeremiah, though the poems name no author. In the older Holy Week services called Tenebrae, Catholics sang Lamentations in the dark, candles going out one by one. Jews read it on Tisha B'Av, the day of mourning for the Temple. Both keep this book for the worst days, because it doesn't pretend. It just finds, in the middle of the alphabet, one thing that hasn't run out.
screen: `I AM THE ONE WHO HAS SEEN AFFLICTION.` · `THIS I CALL TO MIND.` · `RACHAMIM: A MOTHER'S COMPASSION.` · `THE RUINS ARE STILL THERE.` · then, large: `THEY ARE NEW EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day for one mercy that came anyway, in the middle of everything else: a text from someone, hot water, a person who was kind on a bad day. Hold it for a moment, and let tomorrow's first words, before the phone, be thank you for one thing. If you pray, it can be to God, with this line from Lamentations.
rachamim. Hebrew for compassion, kin to the word for womb: the Lord's mercies that aren't used up, but come fresh each morning. Today's word.
Your line: his mercies are new. Not used up, even in the ruins. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics have sung passages of Lamentations at Tenebrae during Holy Week, and some Catholics begin the day with a morning offering or Morning Prayer, thanking God before anything else.

chat.says: How can Lamentations talk about mercy in the middle of all that ruin?
options: It doesn't say the city is fine; it says God's mercies aren't used up, new every morning.
The poet decides the ruin wasn't so bad, and the city will be fine soon.
It says mercy only comes once the walls are rebuilt and the grief is over.
chat.meaning: The ruins are still there. The poet finds one thing that hasn't run out: the Lord's mercies, new every morning, enough for the day.
